content: Acute otitis media (AOM) is a condition that typically resolves on its own, but the pain associated with it is often the most troubling symptom for patients. Recent evidence suggests that antibiotics, once considered the primary treatment, offer less benefit than previously thought. As a result, topical pain relief has emerged as a potentially effective alternative, which may also reduce the overprescription of antibiotics. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effectiveness of topical analgesic treatments for AOM in both adults and children. The search for relevant studies included databases such as the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), Ovid MEDLINE, Ovid EMBASE, EBSCO CINAHL, and Ovid AMED, covering publications up to early 2011. The review focused on double-blind randomized controlled trials (RCTs) or quasi-RCTs that compared otic preparations with analgesic effects (excluding antibiotics) against either placebo or other analgesic otic preparations. The studies included participants with AOM without tympanic membrane perforation, presenting in primary care settings. Three independent reviewers screened the studies, assessed their quality, and extracted data. Attempts to gather additional information from the authors of the included trials were unsuccessful. Ultimately, five trials involving 391 children aged 3 to 18 years met the inclusion criteria. Two of these studies, which included 117 children, compared the use of anesthetic ear drops to placebo at the time of AOM diagnosis. All participants in these studies also received some form of oral pain relief. Across all five studies, it was evident that ear pain generally subsides quickly for most patients. However, a statistically significant reduction in pain was observed in favor of anesthetic ear drops. Specifically, 10 minutes after administration, children using anesthetic drops were more likely to achieve a 50% reduction in pain compared to placebo (risk ratio [RR] 2.13, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.19 to 3.80). This effect was also significant 30 minutes after administration (RR 1.43, 95% CI 1.12 to 1.81). However, no significant difference was observed at the 20-minute mark (RR 1.24, 95% CI 0.88 to 1.74). Three additional trials, involving 274 children, compared anesthetic ear drops to naturopathic herbal ear drops. While naturopathic drops appeared to be favored at 15 and 30 minutes after administration, as well as one to three days after diagnosis, these differences were not statistically significant. Only one trial reported on adverse reactions, and no adverse effects were identified. The overall quality of the evidence from these trials was assessed as being at low or unclear risk of bias. The authors concluded that the limited evidence from these five RCTs suggests that ear drops may provide effective pain relief 30 minutes after administration in older children with AOM. However, the magnitude of this effect remains uncertain, and further high-quality studies are needed to confirm these findings.
